Within the superfamily they occupy three distinct families: canonical protein kinases = d.144.1.7 'Protein kinases, catalytic subunit' (sunid 88854; e.g. cAMP-dependent PK catalytic subunit d1atpe_); aminoglycoside phosphotransferases = d.144.1.6 'APH phosphotransferases' (sunid 64411; e.g. APH(3')-IIIa d1j7la_, plus kanamycin kinase APH(3')-IIa, homoserine kinase ThrB, methylthioribose kinase MtnK and RdoA); phosphoinositide 3-kinases = d.144.1.4 'Phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), catalytic domain' (sunid 56171; e.g. PI3K-gamma d1e8xa4, 1e8x A:726-1092, and the mTOR kinase domain). Pairwise comparison of d1atpe_, d1j7la_ and d1e8xa4 gives 'same_superfamily' in every case with lowest shared node d.144.1; no pair shares a family. Other families in the same superfamily (actin-fragmin kinase d.144.1.3, MHCK/EF2 alpha-kinase d.144.1.5, choline kinase d.144.1.8, RIO1-like d.144.1.9, automated matches d.144.1.0) show how functionally diverse this superfamily is.

What is justified. (1) Common ancestry: superfamily membership in SCOPe is a curated judgement of probable homology based on structure plus shared functional features, so it is justified to conclude that protein kinases, APHs and PI3Ks descend from a common ancestral ATP-dependent phosphotransferase. This is stronger than a fold-only (d.144) relationship, which by itself would not imply homology, but weaker than family-level (d.144.1.x) relationship, which implies clear sequence-detectable relatedness. (2) Shared mechanism at the level of chemistry: a bilobal domain (SCOPe fold comment: 'two alpha+beta domains, C-terminal domain is mostly alpha helical') with ATP bound in the cleft between an N-lobe beta-sheet and a largely helical C-lobe; conserved Mg2+-coordinating residues (catalytic-loop Asp/Asn and the DFG-type Asp), a conserved Lys in the N-lobe positioning the phosphates, and in-line direct transfer of the gamma-phosphate to a hydroxyl acceptor. The superfamily comment notes additional 'functional and structural similarities with the ATP-grasp fold and PIPK', which SCOPe records as a remark, not as classified homology. (3) Therefore it is reasonable to transfer: the identity of the nucleotide-binding site, the general catalytic-base/metal chemistry, and the expectation that ATP-competitive inhibitor scaffolds may cross-react (as wortmannin/LY294002-type and staurosporine-type compounds do between PI3K-related kinases and protein kinases, and as some protein-kinase inhibitors do against APHs).

What is NOT justified by the classification alone. Substrate specificity is not conserved across the superfamily and must not be transferred: d.144.1.7 members phosphorylate Ser/Thr/Tyr hydroxyls on protein substrates; d.144.1.6 APHs phosphorylate hydroxyls of aminoglycoside antibiotics (and the family also contains small-metabolite kinases such as homoserine and methylthioribose kinase); d.144.1.4 members phosphorylate the 3-OH of phosphoinositide lipid headgroups, while mTOR in the same family phosphorylates protein substrates. So even within a single SCOPe family (d.144.1.4) substrate class differs, which shows that family membership, let alone superfamily membership, is not a license to transfer substrate. The substrate-binding surface (activation segment/P+1 loop in protein kinases, the acidic aminoglycoside-binding groove in APHs, the activation loop plus membrane-interacting elements in PI3Ks) is the least conserved part of the domain. Regulation is also family- or protein-specific and non-transferable: activation-loop phosphorylation, regulatory subunits/pseudosubstrates (PKA R-subunit), cyclins, autoinhibitory extensions and allosteric spine assembly are protein-kinase-specific; APHs are constitutively active bacterial resistance enzymes with no such regulation; PI3Ks are regulated by p85/p101-type adaptor subunits, Ras binding and by their own N-terminal domains (the 1e8x chain contains separate SCOPe domains: RBD d1e8xa3 d.15.1.5, C2 d1e8xa2 b.7.1.1, helical/ARM d1e8xa1 a.118.1.6, catalytic d1e8xa4 d.144.1.4), so regulation cannot be inferred from the PK-like domain alone. Evidence required before transferring substrate specificity or regulation. (a) Family-level or closer relationship to a characterised protein: a statistically significant pairwise or profile alignment (HMM/PSI-BLAST) placing the query within the same SCOPe family and ideally the same group/subfamily (d.144.1.7 is explicitly organised into groups and subfamilies), with conservation of the specific substrate-recognition residues (e.g. activation-loop and P+1-loop residues for protein kinases, the aminoglycoside-binding Asp/Glu groove residues for APHs, the lipid-binding activation loop and hVPS34/PIK motifs for PI3Ks). (b) Direct biochemical evidence: in-vitro phosphotransfer assays with the candidate substrates (peptides, aminoglycosides, phosphoinositides), steady-state kinetics (kcat/KM) and product identification by mass spectrometry or 32P/TLC. (c) Structural evidence of the specific complex: a crystal/cryo-EM structure or validated model with substrate or substrate-analogue bound, and mutagenesis of the proposed recognition residues. (d) For regulation: evidence of the regulatory partners and modifications in the organism of interest (regulatory subunit co-purification/interaction assays, phosphosite mapping of the activation loop, genetic or cellular readouts), plus domain-architecture analysis of the full-length protein, since regulatory behaviour is encoded largely outside the catalytic domain. (b) Direct biochemical evidence: in-vitro phosphotransfer assays with the candidate substrates (peptides, aminoglycosides, phosphoinositides), steady-state kinetics (kcat/KM) and product identification by mass spectrometry or 32P/TLC. (c) Structural evidence of the specific complex: a crystal/cryo-EM structure or validated model with substrate or substrate-analogue bound, and mutagenesis of the proposed recognition residues. (d) For regulation: evidence of the regulatory partners and modifications in the organism of interest (regulatory subunit co-purification/interaction assays, phosphosite mapping of the activation loop, genetic or cellular readouts), plus domain-architecture analysis of the full-length protein, since regulatory behaviour is encoded largely outside the catalytic domain. (e) Where inhibitor cross-reactivity is the question, direct binding/IC50 measurements, because ATP-site conservation only predicts possible, not actual, cross-inhibition.
